rv.q: Jane Alexander and James Cromwell deliver a miniature master class in the art of slyly ambiguous acting
For the most part, though, Grand Horizons is a sweet, sweet delight.
But in Leigh Silverman's production for Second Stage, the gifted cast—which also includes Maulik Pancholy as Brian's would-be hookup and Priscilla Lopez as a blowsy neighbor—keeps the energy high.
All of the performances are great and Silverman's directing emphasizes the performances without skimping on showmanship.
The gags are not as slick as Simon at his best, but they have a dark, cruel depth more appropriate to our own time and our own ineffable anxiety about old age and loneliness.
For those few minutes, at least, Grand Horizons achieves a poignancy and depth that have otherwise eluded it.

Unfortunately, her realization that she can no longer tell the requisite wifely lies — the ones that say her husband and children are infinitely excusable — comes too late in her life, as too late in the play.
Bess Wohl's comedy about the breakup of a couple living in a senior community is humorous, but just barely.
But “Grand Horizons” delivers old-fashioned entertainment that’s become a rarity on Broadway.
The comedy and drama in Grand Horizons work in clever interplay.
Their characters may be at odds, but these two are a match made in theatrical heaven.
Grand Horizons may not be as weighty as some of Wohl's other works, but it's damn funny, and very on-point.
Back and forth the play goes—sometimes silly, sometimes deadly serious.
Best efforts and a sweet heart notwithstanding, Grand Horizons falls short of its expansive title.
Precisely what Wohl is chasing remains elusive.
With Grand Horizons, she seems to have wanted to step back and try her hand at a traditional, non-challenging, old-fashioned sex comedy.

A brief, but extremely effective and very funny opening scene, shows how, after more than 50 years of marriage, their lives are pretty much on silent automatic pilot. It's no spoiler to mention that the silence of their dinner is broken by Nancy calmly informing her husband, "I think I would like a divorce.
But the play’s horizons are too easy and narrow.
